subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING TRACKS AND PREMISES AT SAINT JOHN
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING TRACKS AND PREMISES AT SAINT JOHN
speechtext:
The object of this bill is to ratify and confirm an agreement between His Majesty the King and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the joint use of certain tracks and premises belonging to His Majesty at Saint John, New Brunswick, and thus validating the agreement for a full period of 99 years from the first day of January, 1927, unless sooner terminated in accordance with the provisions of the agreement. Neither this bill nor either of the other two that follow has anything to do with last year's legislation; they are bills which date from an earlier period, this one from 1927 and the other two from 1912 and 1915. I mention this in order to clear the air, because I have been asked a number of times w'hether this had to do with last year's legislation.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

On the orders of the day:

May I ask the Secretary of State whether any progress has been made in regard to the proposed revision of the Companies Act in accordance with the agreements reached or reported to have been reached at the interprovincial conference ?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
The hon. member gave me notice of this question and I presume it is asked in view of certain telegrams which have appeared in the press purporting to emanate from the Department of the Attorney General of Quebec. At the meeting of the interprovincial conference in January last, a report was made of the understanding reached at a meeting of the representatives of the attorneys general of the several provinces or their deputies to consider a draft Companies Act which had been prepared at the office of the Secretary of State and submitted to them for their consideration. That reports reads as follows:
The law officers of the several provinces or their deputies met Thursday, January 18th, to consider a draft Companies Act which had been submitted to them by the Secretary of State.
Representatives of several of the provinces suggested that they would probably retain the form of act which has already been adopted
74726-74J
by their respective legislatures, such as incorporation by letters patent, or by memorandum of association or by grant from the crown; but that this would not preclude the acceptance by all the provinces of the material provisions of such a bill as may be agreed upon.
After a general discussion of the scope of the draft bill then presented, the unanimous opinion was expressed by the provincial representatives that the law officers of the several provinces should, on or before March 1 next, send to the Secretary of State suggestions of such amendments or changes in the draft bill as they might deem expedient, and that, thereafter, the Secretary of State should convene at Ottawa such law officers or their representatives as could conveniently attend, for a further discussion of proposed amendments or changes in the draft bill; and that, in the meantime, the draft bill should not be widely distributed nor introduced to the parliament of Canada for public discussion.
That report was unanimously adopted at the conference. A few days later the department of the Secretary of State sent a copy of that report, together with additional copies of the draft bill, to the attorneys general of the several provinces, with a suggestion that on or before March 1 next they should send to the Secretary of State suggestions of such amendments or changes in the draft bill as might be deemed expedient. No suggestions have been received from the department of the attorney general of either of the provinces, and no reply has been received to that letter which was so sent.
This morning there appeared in the public press despatches from Quebec, from one of which appearing in the Gazette this morning. I read as follows:
Chas. Lanctot, K.C., deputy attorney-general, returned here to-day from a conference at 1 oronto with the Hon. W. H. Price, attorney-general, at which conference the draft of the federal legislation was studied, and the decision come to that it did not meet the wishes of the provinces, nor carry out the conception of the provincial authorities at the inter-provmcial conference as to what uniform Companies Act Ottawa had in mind.
It will be recalled that at the 1933 interprovincial conference there was agreement that the time had come to have uniformity in legislation as regards companies, it having been admitted that the disparity as between legislation of the provinces, and of Ottawa, has been of a nature to constitute "bidding" for a compiinies incorporation. The federal authorities m 1933 agreed to draft a uniform act which would apply to all, and this draft was submitted at the inter provincial conference held last January.
Premier Taschereau, speaking in the legislative assembly, following this recent conference, expressed the view that agreement had been reached, that Ottawa would' bring in its legislation this session, and the provinces follow suit. He told the house there were only minor differences to be adjusted.
Motions for Papers

Mr. Lanctot and Hon. Mr. Price, however, found at Toronto this week that the ideas of Ottawa are not suitable in a number of respects and hence decided that there must be further adjustments of the different viewpoints. To this end the intention is that there shall be a committee representing the provincial governments named, and they will discuss by correspondence what should be done, and come to a decision during the course of the present year, and then acquaint Ottawa with their joint viewpoint.

My own view was that the agreement was not perhaps as provident as it might have been, because my view is that if a young fellow can save $500-and apparently some of them are doing it-perhaps he would be following the course of wisdom if he did not start in to borrow, but instead saved another S5C0. May I

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There have been no direct suggestions to the Canadian government. Various schemes have been talked about, but no definite plan has been suggested by anybody to the government. The Imperial parliament has discussed the matter of empire migration on many occasions, and we are all acquainted with the difficulties that are associated with any plan to distribute the people of the empire throughout the dominions. We know what has happened in a measure in Canada during the last few years, as well as in Australia, from which country a great many more people have returned to Great Britain than migrated. I offer it as a suggestion, whether the outline of any plan comes before me or before anyone who may follow me, that any scheme or plan had better be looked at from very long range and gone into with the utmost care. It has been said on many occasions by men in high places, as well as by others, that we are not attracting British agriculturists to Canada. Well, Mr. Chairman, anyone who makes that statement has little conception of the situation that obtains in the United Kingdom, where perhaps less than seven per cent of the population are agriculturists of a desirable type. It is most difficult to attract from the United Kingdom to Canada an agriculturist who is doing well there; no country wants to give up that type of agriculturist. So I say that any plan for the migration of people, no matter how desirable it may appear, should be examined with the utmost care. No such scheme has been placed before the government, however.

I ask for that information because I believe that until this country reaches the stage that has been reached in Great Britain in social legislation in the past twenty-five years immigration is out of the question. It is out of the question to people in the old land where there is unemployment insurance, health insurance, besides widows' pensions and many
other forms of social legislation such as we find there; they cannot be expected to come to a country where they are more or less left to their own resources without protection in case of unemployment and adversity. I said: A man from Canada. I have heard it said by some people, I do not know by whom, that those in opposition are supposed to offer congratulations to the government when they are doing right and to give helpful suggestions. I rise at this time to say to the Acting Minister of Immigration that I am fully in accord with the position he has taken with respect to immigration to Canada. He has, however, suggested that we might wait until such time as a concrete system of immigration is offered to the government. I do not agree there because that might be too late. Inasmuch as gentlemen in another house of parliament, that at Westminster, have, because of their action in carrying a resolution, not hesitated to say to the people of Great Britain and Canada what their views are with respect to emigration from the British isles to this country, this is an opportune time for us in 
Canada to say something as to what we might approve in this country.	_
When I said that I rose, because of being m opposition, to be helpful to the minister, my mind went back to around 1929; it could go back further, but it went back more especially to 1929 when the present Prime Minister sat on this side in opposition and advocated that the more people we brought to Canada, the more work and employment there would be for those who were in this country; when the Minister of Railways said that Canada might be the meoca for the surplus people of the whole world if we had a proper government and a proper fiscal policy; when the organizer of the Conservative party, General McRae, then member for Vancouver North, advocated bringing either 250,000 or 300,000 families to this country at an expense of $300,000,000, or $30,000,000 a year for ten years, and when that glorious old Tory, the Hon. Howard Ferguson, was making a trip through Europe canvassing the various countries there to send their surplus people to this province and criticizing the then government because we were too careful in our selection of the type of immigrant we wanted to come here. I am wondering where that policy has gone. Why the change? There is now in office a government that is satisfactory to the Minister of Railways, a government that, I hope, has a policy that is satisfactory to him; and he said that if we had that policy and that government, this country should be a mecca for the surplus people of the whole world. What is the trouble now? I would say to the Minister of Railways that I am glad he has changed his view. Responsibility is a great thing.
So is irresponsibility.

I am not entirely blaming the Minister of Railways because that was the general view of the Conservative party when they were in opposition. The Conservative press throughout the country lambasted the government of the day, pointing out that we were trying to hold Canada in a narrow channel and to restrict immigration. We have heard the Acting Minister of Immigration this afternoon speak of the proportion of agriculturists to be found in Great Britain. Anyone who knows anything about industrial England is well aware that very few people in that country are engaged in agriculture and that you cannot make an agricultural out of an industrial population. So where are we to get these agriculturists and what were we to do with them when we got them here?
I think the Acting Minister of Immigration and the government should tell General Hornby what we propose to do in this country. Who is financing him? Is it the British government or some select few people who want to get rid of the unemployed population, trafficking in humanity, throwing people from one country to another? Is that the game in which Canada is to be engaged? General Hornby appearing before labour people in the city of Winnipeg has a plan all set out for so many thousand people to be settled in certain communities and all that sort of thing. He has even provision made for their return to Great Britain if they do not make good. How are our Canadian workers to be safeguarded so that these immigrants will return to Great Britain? All these questions must be taken into consideration.
I say again that I congratulate the Acting Minister of Immigration and the Conservative government on their right about face on the immigration question. I think I can congratulate the Conservative press because, since this government came into power, they realized it could not provide work for the people who are here much less for those it might bring in from outside.
In conclusion, I hope the minister will view and continue to view with alarm any proposals that are made by anybody outside Canada.

I think at that time everyone in Canada, Mr. Beatty, Sir Henry Thornton, nearly all the business men and most of the politicians, including my hon. friends who were then in power, were taking the attitude that we should bring immigrants to this country. No one then thought that in the following October the world was going to be overtaken by the greatest depression that had ever occurred, and that it was going to continue for four years. I take the attitude now that when the depression is over, when Canada is once more on the upgrade-it is now to my mind, but not back to normal at all-when it is back to normal I believe Canada will require more immigrants. I do not believe that this country with three and a half million square miles, double the whole area of Europe exclusive of Russia, will continue to limit its population to the ten millions in the country at the present time.
I believe the time will come when, normal conditions being restored, we will again bring immigrants to this country and be able to absorb them. I do not wish now, especially in the discussion of my hon. colleague's estimates, to get into any debate on this subject, but I desire just to point out, as I did yesterday in Montreal, what is my firm conviction. I mentioned also, without criticizing my hon. friends-because I said everyone at that time advocated bringing in immigrants-that my hon. friends in three years during their regime brought in 436,000 immigrants. They were proceeding in accordance with my belief at that time that we should bring immigrants to this country, because conditions were good. In rising, sffi to take part in this debate, I have no intention of delivering a speech which might serve, perhaps, in ten years, when the world will have again settled' down to normal conditions. Under the present circumstances, we should refuse to participate in the colonization policy of the Empire and not encourage it by contributions to send settlers who would certainly become a burden to this country. The government must be aware that, for the last three years, it has been unable to provide for the needs of our unemployed. It behooves the government to place the little money which remains at the disposal of our fellow-citizens and not contribute to again increase the number of unemployed.
That is why I am opposed to this item of $10,000 to participate in this colonization plan. Members on the government side who hail from Quebec and who have, for the last three years, been criticizing, on hustings, the former regime for having fostered immigration in this country, must have been shocked in learning to-day, in the house, that their friends are ready to foster immigration to Canada, even in these times of depression.
I wish to protest, sir, against the expenditure of $10,000 and I request the government to put into practice what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has been preaching for the last three years: "Canada First." Let us endeavour to first help our fellow-citizens to earn a livelihood and let us leave in their own country those who have not the means to settle in Canada.

He said that only seven per cent of the British people are engaged in agriculture, therefore good agriculturists could not very readily be made out of the other ninety-three per cent. I take exception to that statement; some of the best
[Mr. Manion.l

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy Raver quoted from the famous speech made on May 22, 1929, by the present Minister of Railways, who says that during the years we were in office we brought in 436,000-

The last three calendar
years, I said.

That makes it that much worse'. He now asserts that this government has admitted only 60,000. Let us see how that compares with the statement quoted by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. If the farming country is as prosperous as the Prime Minister and some of his followers claim, we should be able to absorb hundreds of thousands of all classes of immigrants from all countries. How then does he justify his present commendation of this government's position in admitting only 60,000?

Simply >by world conditions, that is all. I did not criticize the late government for bringing in that number, and I said so; I simply pointed out that they had brought so many in and we had cut the number down to 60,000, giving round figures from memory. As a matter of fact this government has been forced to reduce the number, not because I do not believe every word I said then, but because of world conditions, a depression such as the world never experienced before, and in which we share.

All I wish to say is that in May 1929 the present Minister of Railways made that statement. In 1930 he and his colleagues in the present administration went about the country preaching blue ruin, and to-day he is Minister of Railways simply because of that. They spoke of the deplorable conditions existing in Canada, and said that it was not a world condition but peculiarly a Canadian condition; there was no depression in Europe, they said. Why', the depression in Europe was four y'ears old at that time, before it ever struck Canada.
I did not discuss the depression in Europe at all. I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about.

In 1930 the hon. member said it was peculiarly a Canadian condition.

Due to the policy of the Canadian government.
Oh, nonsense.
In every speech he made.

It seems so many want to talk to the minister that I am not going to be privileged to say much more. But I just want to put the minister straight on this, that his attitude in May, 1929, was that we should bring in hundreds of thousands of immigrants from all countries.
You were doing it.

Then on the 5th day of March, 1934, he stands up and excuses this government by telling us that we brought in 460,000 immigrants at the very time he was telling us we should have brought in hundreds of thousands more. Now he says, in appreciation of this government, that they brought in only 60,000. I hope that when the government goes to the country, which probably will be this year, his attitude will be different -as I know it will-from his attitude in 1930. They pulled that stunt, to use the vernacular, in 1930, but it cannot be repeated in 1934.

The thing that impressed
' me in this discussion, after listening to the Minister of Railways and his recognition of the fact that there was a period of great prosperity before this government came into power, no matter who was responsible for it, was my recollection of the vicious, bitter, uncalled for .attacks that were made upon the Minister of Immigration of the previous government. I may say to hon. members of the house who are here lor the first time that if they have thought sometimes the government opposite have been subjected to severe criticism, they should have sat in this parliament from 1922 to 1930. We all remember the attack made upon the government with regard to the customs department; we all recall the bitter attacks made upon the then Minister of Immigration, and if I am ever disposed, as I sometimes am, to let up on my criticism of the present government, my thoughts go back to the attacks made upon the late Hon. Robert Forke when he was Minister of Immigration. It was not only the private members of the then opposition who attacked him; I cannot forget how the present Prime Minister spoke of the late Hon. Robert Forke as a man who was temperamentally unfitted for the great position which he held. A whole session was devoted by the opposition to attacks upon that gentleman.

Just along the line of
what my hon. friend has said, on Thursday night I was greatly tempted to rise and recite just what the hon. member for Lisgar has stated the present Prime Minister said across the floor of the house to the then Minister of Immigration; I should have done so had it not been for the esteem in which we all hold the present Minister of National Revenue. We all remember the Prime Minister saying: "Why can you not remember it?" and " Why, Mr. Chairman, what a spectacle; a minister of the crown not able to give the information." We were too kind on Thursday night, in sheer deference to the new Minister of National Revenue, but as the hon. member for Lisgar says, sometimes we get a little warm under the collar when we listen to hon. gentlemen opposite now that they are sitting to the right of the speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: If I might put my hon. friend right, there has been no such number of deportations. I think the number would run closer to 16,000.

According to a return tabled by the minister on February 15, the figure is about 26,000, of whom over 13,000 were British subjects. Coming back to General Hornby's scheme, may I say that this man has been going across the country addressing boards of trade, Canadian clubs and other organizations, creating the impression that there is a big scheme under way to bring immigrants to this country. He has caused a great deal of unrest in many localities, and I should like to ask the minister if he does not think it would be advisable for him, as Minister of Immigration, to give to the press a statement pointing out that there is no foundation to this scheme and that this government has not encouraged it in any way. I think it would be a good thing, because it would relieve the erroneous impression that has gone abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: What is his scheme?
I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Neither do I. Am I to give a statement to the press condemning a scheme when I know nothing about it?
If General Hornby interviewed the minister a couple of times the minister must have some idea of the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I said he did not have a very clear idea when he saw me.
If he is getting locations of land and so on, surely the department could find out about his scheme.
The department is not a police force.

Well, they have a certain responsibility. To-day thousands of people cannot find work and cannot get enough to eat, but the impression has been going out that under this scheme thousands of immigrants will be brought to Canada to settle in different parts of the country. With all respect I think the minister should issue a statement denying these reports.
Did I understand the minister to say that he does not know the Hornby scheme, a British migration movement, that has been discussed with the different provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I do not.

I have an outline of the scheme here if the committee would like to hear it; it is very brief. With regard to Prince Edward Island General Hornby says that he has not yet visited that province at the request of the government, but that he intended to do so at the very earliest opportunity after his return to eastern Canada. With regard to Nova Scotia two locations have been selected and the approval of the provincial government has been obtained. In New Brunswick there are two selected locations, and again the approval of the provincial government has been given. In Quebec two locations have been chosen but approval has not been given. In Ontario four locations have been selected, in the counties of Middlesex, Oxford, Brant and Glengarry and Stormont. No approval has been given as yet. In Manitoba two locations have been provisionally accepted, but the approval of the government has not been given. In Saskatchewan the number of locations selected is four. Approval has been given by the Saskatchewan government to those four locations. I understand one of them is at Lashburn, a short distance from North Battleford. In Alberta the number of selections is six; no approval has yet been given, but negotiations are of course going on between General Hornby and the provincial government. In British Columbia the number of locations selected is one; no approval has yet been given.
Then, following these locations in the nine provinces this statement is made in the memorandum broadcast by General Hornby:
The above mentioned twenty-three settlements, each to consist of one hundred farms are the first instalment of what will undoubtedly become a great overseas migration movement from the old country-a voluntary, spontaneous and continuous movement, involving eventually the establishment of no less than 250 such community settlements, 25,000 farms in all, absorbing at the outset 25,000 new settler families, 125,000 persons, and maintaining an uninterrupted flow of at least 5,000 families. 25,000 persons, to Canada every year. Every county in the United Kingdom, and every town of importance should have its community settlement in Canada, to take care of its selected immigrants.
For the next few months in Canada our work will be confined to the lining up of the farms to make up the proposed settlement at each of the twenty-three selected locations.
But these are only a forerunner of a large movement which is to take place from year to year after these locations have been definitely settled, approval given by provincial governments and all details worked out.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to say any more, but may I add simply this: that

Supply-Immigration-Empire Settlement
if file department at Ottawa through the minister has not had this policy of General Hornby presented to it, apparently the federal government is either directly or indirectly linked up with it. For instance, in the memorandum from which I have been reading I find information which I believe the minister should have, and which I am quite pleased to give him. It is as follows:
For the same reason I welcome the step taken by the federal government in placing the services of the staffs of the land settlement department and the soldier settlement department at the disposal of the provincial governments, for the purpose of making surveys and reports, where required.
There is a definite link up between the Department of Immigration and Colonization of the national government with the colonization departments of the different provincial governments. Consequently I think the headquarters at Ottawa ought to have all the facts and all the details of this policy to give to the house, so that information may toe given not only to parliament but to the country.
Shall the item carry?
No.

May I ask the minister
if this authority was given to -the soldier settlement board, and to the land settlement board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Officials of the soldier
settlement board, who are really the land settlement branch of the immigration department, since we started colonization at home, have been constantly at work endeavouring to tabulate, so far as possible, suitable available lands for colonization. It is a difficult task, because many of these lands are privately owned. I have not had the officials of the department go to the trouble of tabulating these lands in any great detail, because of necessity they change from week to week and from month to month. But if General Hornby or General anybody else wants to go to the department and get all the information they have in matters of this kind, he is at perfect liberty to do so.
I can say only this, that I am amazed at some hon. members going to the length of utter condemnation of British settlement in Canada, because I by no means agree with the view that the right type of British settler would not be a very welcome person in Canada, and I should not like to see the time when he would not foe welcome. Remember, there are other schemes constantly affecting
and concerning settlement in Canada. We have the community settlements of western Canada, which have grown up in the last fifteen years, and we have other types of settlement, both assisted and unassisted. To the extent that our predecessors in office put forth their activities towards inviting and encouraging the right sort and type of settler to come to Canada, I have no complaint. But I do have a complaint which I shall now register, in case I have not done so before, that when I took over the administration of the Department of Immigration there were permits granted to hon. members on both sides of this chamber, to railway companies, to various agencies of all kinds and characters. Remember, there was not just one man's name on a permit, and information showing where that man's background was investigated, but on one sheet of paper there would be authorization for admission of large numbers and these were sent to Europe and traded in among the steamship lines at so much a head. That is the kind of immigration I condemn and will continue to condemn.
But I commend the late government to the extent that their activities were conducted- and they were in some measure-towards the invitation given to the right type of person to settle in Canada. They are entitled to that commendation, and I have no hesitation in giving it.

Mr. Chairman, having sat in this house since 1921 I find it interesting to listen to this discussion on immigration. Fortunately or unfortunately I happened to be Minister of Immigration at a time somewhat similar to the present. At that time the force and eloquence of the opposition were directed to the desirability of widening the field for immigration, and of the expenditure of more money for that purpose in order to bring in more immigrants. Not only that, but the financial houses in eastern Canada, and the railway companies, were putting up money for the purpose of encouraging people to come to Canada. Sometimes I have been incensed when, sitting in this house, I have listened to the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite who, on the occasion to which I have referred, were most vociferous in their declarations that the government was not doing its duty and was not getting more people to come to Canada.
Let me say now, as I said in 1921, that I do not believe the Canadian government should spend a dollar in bringing immigrants into Canada. Any man who is worth his salt

Supply-Immigration-Empire Settlement
and wants to come to Canada could be examined, but we should get away from the idea of inviting people to come to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: We are not at the present time.

No, I know you are not at the present time. With one exception I am not complaining about what is happening now. When the minister states that he believes British settlement would be worth while, I agree, but when we listen to the returns to which references were made by the hon. member for Provencher we find that fewer continentals than Britishers were returned. I wish to bring that to the attention of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I gave the explanation.

But I may also direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that not in this house but outside of it, much of the difficulty experienced in the present day with respect to unemployment was brought about by the uncontrolled flow of immigration into Canada in former times. If it was uncontrolled my hon.friends opposite must take their fair share of the responsibility because there was only one group in this house, which sat in the far corner to my left, which from the day it entered the house consistently up until this moment opposed immigration into Canada. The Conservative party, on the other hand, backed by the financial interests of eastern Canada and the transportation interests, were continually driving any government and any minister who would listen to them into unlimited immigration. It was the only way in which we could pay our public debt; that was the argument, but unfortunately these immigrants, and it is no reflection upon them to say so, have become a burden to us to-day rather than a help in paying our public debt. This is not the first time that ministers have had to sit back and take a castigation over immigration, not by a long shot, and a castigation from the very gentlemen who now seek to adopt a defensive attitude. It is just as well that they be reminded of this once in a while because I had to take my share when hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting over here. I sat for four days where the Minister of Immigration is now sitting, listening to sixty-five members in the far left corner of the house demanding that the immigration estimates be cut in two if not abolished altogether, because we had no place in Canada for immigrants, while from the Conservative benches in this house, then the opposition, there was a most vociferous

demand for increased immigration all along the line. I need only remind hon. gentlemen opposite that as late as 1927 or 1928 the then member for Vancouver, now Senator McRae, propounded a scheme to the house which if it had been put into effect would only have added to our present difficulties. So I say that hon. gentlemen opposite are not warranted in the criticism which they are levelling against the government that preceded them in office. True, the late Hon. Mr. Forke when Minister of Immigration entered into agreements with the railway companies to bring people to this country, but it was done upon the insistent demand of hon. gentlemen opposite then sitting on this side of the house, and various organizations throughout the country, churches and everybody else, were behind that demand. Now we are all agreed that that policy was a mistake; for we have a very serious state of affairs in this country. The present difficult position in which we find ourselves is not by any means due entirely to immigration, because in comparison with the number of people in Canada our immigration during the last eight or ten years did not amount to very much. I shall have something to say later, Mr. Chairman, as to other causes for our present conditions, but this is not the time or place to enter into such a discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I happened to be in the House of Commons wdien the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) was Minister of Immigration, and I remember the debates to which he has made reference. I challenge him to say that at any time the official Conservative opposition of that day ever advocated uncontrolled immigration into this country.
As late as 1929.
Not uncontrolled; we urged selected immigration.
What about General McRae's scheme?

His scheme was never crystallized in the form of resolutions, and was never the policy of the Conservative opposition. As to the criticism of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) he himself never had any concrete policy on immigration. I remember him standing in his place in this row and making a speech, seven hours in length, if I recollect aright, and when he got through no one knew what his policy was, not even himself, and I leave it to my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) if I am not right.

He must have been a good man.

The
trouble was that the government had no well formulated plan in those days, and they were bringing in people who did not stay here. We had the spectacle in this country of one million Canadians leaving Canada under the regime of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, and they brought in about as many immigrants from continental Europe.
The only reason they do not leave now is that they cannot get out.

That
would be too bad if it deprived my hon. friend of any assistance. My reply to the hon. gentleman who has been scolding the minister is this, that when he was Minister of Immigration his government spent all kinds of money to bring people into Canada, and then by a policy of attrition, wearing down the industries of this country, they drove out the immigrants they had brought in, or drove out our own people, and Canada lost just that many. Through the policy or lack of policy on the part of the late government we lost millions of Canadians whom we shall never replace.

You are
getting them back.
No. Some of them will never come back. We also had a lot of southern Europeans brought into this country who never should have been brought in.
We are feeding over one million people in this country through the policies of this government.

These are the key
men who run the whole institution, and they have to be prepared to instruct and administer

the whole militia force. There is no increase in them. It has been generally felt by every government since we have had a country at all that we must have a military force, and so long as we have a military force we must have a head and a staff to administer it. We must however keep the administrative divisions ready and capable at all times.

We had all the military districts as at present except Regina. During the war one was formed at Regina, and one was also formed at St. John.
Are any of the officers who come under this vote used as supervisors of relief camps?
No.

There is a certain

I want to join with the hon. member for Melville in objecting to this vote. We have a reduction of 3170,000 in the money being voted for militia purposes whereas there is a total reduction of over
8800,000	in the estimates for agriculture. I object to this vote. I am one of those who cannot see why, in times like these, we should not reduce this vote for military purposes. When you live in a district where the people

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Mines):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It is unfortunate, but the number of survey parties had to be reduced very materially because economies had to be made. The parties for this year's operations and the places where they will go have not yet been finally determined and probably will not be for three weeks or a month. Officials of the department and I have been as careful as we can to see that the parties are so arranged that there will be no interruption in the continuity of the geological survey work. Of course I am hopeful, as I am sure every member is, that the time will not be too long delayed when additional parties over and above those that are now being sent out will go out as times improve. Arrangements for the work of the summer have not yet been perfected.
How have the survey parties been allocated? By provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In the past the parties have been allocated not according to provinces, that is by reason of any demand or pressure from them, but purely to make a continuous projection of geological work. Of course my hon. friend knows that the geological surveys of Canada were started officially in 1842 and have proceeded from that time on, having regard to those areas where it would seem that the projection of geological surveys would result in the greatest good; but they have not been allocated to provinces as such. There is one province, I think, British Columbia, where according to statute these surveys must be carried on. But the arrangement made is: first, to see that the continuity of the geological survey is not disturbed; second, to see that the geological surveys are carried on where they will disclose the beat areas for prospecting and so forth, and, third, to arrange with those provinces which have provincial geological surveys so that our work does not overlap theirs. That practice was pursued by the hon. member for West Edmonton and it is a very proper one.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

I have not the figures
available at the moment, but if the hon. member has any difficulty in getting them I can either furnish them before the estimates for this department are concluded or give them to him personally.

I thank the hon. gentleman very much, and as he cannot give it to the committee right now I will give it myself. The decrease in the value of production of metals including gold, and of non-ferrous metal products for 1932 as compared with 1930, is $108,691,098. Why have we a decrease in the value of those minerals? Now that the minister has the figure it will be easy for him to tell the committee. At the same time I will ask what minerals are included in that list.

635 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There are many factors that affect the value of mineral production. One would be the very low prices for copper, lead and zinc. My hon. friend knows that copper, for instance, dropped from 24 cents to less than 4 cents per pound, and while in

Supply-Mines
lead and zinc the reduction was not so marked yet there was a very great contraction in the price of those metals. Gold, on the other hand, increased in world price. As I said a moment ago, it could scarcely in fairness be anticipated that I would have available on short notice the figures asked for, but 1 will have them before these estimates are passed.

I thank the hon. gentleman, and I ask him if he would be kind enough to tell the house if that decrease in value of production means a decrease in labour employed, and if so, how many miners have been put out of work on account of it? That is one question. Then I would ask if the exports of the minerals I have mentioned have been larger in quantity although smaller in value?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will have to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce for those figures; or if he would wish that I get them for him I shall be glad to do so.

Thank you. Now we will
take another classification of minerals in the same item:
Value of lion-metallic minerals and structural materials production; and value of nonmetallic mineral products, except glass.
This is a description which comes from the bureau of statistics; what are the nonmetallic minerals and structural materials? If the hon. gentleman would be kind enough to give that information I would be thankful.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It is quite obvious that
the figures requested by the hon. gentleman come within the purview of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Of course there are parts of the interrogation that I can answer, with respect to structural material, that is brick, building stone and things of that character, the investigation of which falls within the purview of the Mines department. The marketing of these materials, how much is exported and imported, and the values and so on do not come within the activities of the Mines department.

I understand that asbestos is included in the non-metallic minerals. The minister has said that these figures come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I must tell him that I obtained these figures from the bureau of statistics, but they came from the Department of Mines; they were certified by one of the employees who comes directly under the jurisdiction of the
hon. gentleman. Therefore I will ask him with regard to the value of non-metallic minerals, structural materials and so on. What was the value of the production of these minerals in 1932 as compared with 1930; is there a decrease or an increase and, if so, why? I see the hon. gentleman is not going to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Oh, yes; I will answer.
The statistics the Mines department has concerning the production, the values, the imports and exports of these materials were procured from the bureau of statistics. I cannot follow the hon. member for Temiseouata when he says that the bureau base their figures on certifications from the Mines department. There may be something of which we have some special knowledge but generally, and I think entirely, we rely upon the bureau if we need statistics of that character.

I thank the hon. gentleman, but I may tell him how I proceed when I want statistics. I do not write to any particular employee of the bureau; I write to the Dominion Statistician who refers my letter to some of his officials. When we ask questions about different departments we receive answers certified by different people. In this instance the report on the value of the mineral production of Canada was certified by a gentleman whose name I have not here but who signed as chief of the mines branch. Perhaps it was the mines branch of the bureau of statistics, but I was induced to believe that he was under the jurisdiction of the hon. gentleman.
At all events we have a Department of Mines. The minister is very genial, but this question of minerals is of the utmost importance to Canada. Here we have the products of the land, of the sea and of the mines, and we cannot neglect any of them. I do not insist on an answer with regard to these figures, but I will put them on Hansard so that each member may draw his own conclusions. In 1932 the value of production of non-metallic minerals and structural materials except glass was $203,599,158. In 1930 the value was $307,710,915, showing a decrease in 1932 of $104,151,757, which means that the people engaged in cutting stone, in quarrying, in the mine shafts and so on have suffered a great loss. I agree that these matters could be discussed under the items of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but they come mainly under the estimates of my hon. friend. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has general supervision over the trade of this country, but these matters are

Supply-M ines

of particular interest to the house at the present time. In the same way this afternoon we discussed the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
There is still another item which is of the utmost importance. I refer to the value of glass production, including pressed and blown glass and the bevelling, cutting and so on of plate glass. In 1932 the value of this production was 88,469,895 as compared with $12,191,752 in 1930, or a decrease of $3,721,857. For that small industry such a reduction represents a panic. In the same category we find the value of chemical production; in 1930 this amounted to $119,969,637, while in 1932 it had dropped to $95,279,376, or a decrease of $24,690,261. What about the home market? Prices are falling all the time, and with these figures it is easy to see why so many miners are unemployed.
Another important item is iron and steel and their products; this is a very large Canadian industry. We have the British Empire Steel Corporation in Cape Breton, the Algoma Steel Corporation in Ontario and other large plants, and this is a matter of interest in many provinces. In 1932 the value of this production was $226,205,543, while in 1930 it was $569,745,973, a decrease in 1932 of $343,540,432. The total decrease in the value of the production of the articles I have mentioned is $584,795,205. It is almost inconceivable that mineral production has decreased by over $584,000,000. My hon. friends opposite can check my figures, because they may be found at page 635 of Hansard. I reecived them from the government, either the Department of Mines or the Department Df Trade and Commerce, through the bureau Df statistics.

The information is not
detailed. I shall take the liberty of asking the minister to give me some explanation in that connection. I am ready to hear him, if he is kind enough to speak, because I asked about the value of mineral production and I received an answer about the value of iron and steel products. The last line of the information contains this expression, "decrease, $343,540,432." If this figure concerns primary industry, all right, but I wish to know. I do not say it is all right because I am satisfied with it; I am very sorry about it, and I am sure the hon. gentleman himself is very sorry. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The items we have under
review at the moment have nothing whatever to do with the sale of mineral, precious or otherwise, but have to do, purely, with the scientific investigations of the Mines department, which deal with ore dressing, metallurgy and geological surveys, which are self-explanatory. Although I have no figures, nor has my department the figures to which the hon. member for Temiscouata has addressed himself, I would say that the larger figure would cover the manufactured article. While I do know the hon. member is deeply concerned with the possibility of miners being out of work, the fact is that with the exception of certain places connected with the coal mining industry of Canada, miners are not out of work. In fact, in a number of places it is very difficult to obtain the services of experienced miners who can carry on the work in the rapidly expanding precious metal mining operations of Canada. I can but repeat that it is not the function of the Department of Mines to collect and tabulate the figures to which the hon. gentleman has referred. That is a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have no doubt those figures could quite easily be determined, and if I can be of any assistance to the hon. member in getting them together I should be very glad to do so. As far as these items are concerned the Department of Mines does not engage in the sale of or advertise for the sale of the minerals, but does try to solve under the first item, the metallurgical problems with which miners are met; under the second item, the projection of geological surveys, in order that they may reach the hands of the prospectors and the mining fraternity generally, and the publication of reports. I am not prepared to go into the figures to which the hon. member has made reference, because they do not come within the compass of the activities of the Department of Mines.

I thank the hon. member
for his courtesy. I shall not insist, therefore, but will take advantage of his generous offer to supply me with more information. I have approached the matter with an open mind, and shall be thankful to him if he is kind enough to assist me in obtaining the desired information.

I should like to ask the minister one or two questions in connection with the vote now before the committee concerning geological surveys, and particularly about those surveys in British Columbia. There may be a general decline in the value of minerals produced throughout

Supply-Mines
Canada, but I have the honour to represent a district in which there is a very substantial increase in the amount of minerals being produced, and a section in which there is intense activity. In addition to that I wish to remind the minister that by statute the federal government is obliged to take charge of all the geological work there may be in British Columbia. I regret very much that conditions are such that it has been found necessary to reduce this vote, as I consider it one of the most important in the estimates now before us, so far as British Columbia is concerned. I should like to ask the minister if it is not possible to continue the geological surveys in that part of British Columbia particularly where theTe is intense activity in the search for gold. I refer to the Cariboo and Bridge River areas, both of which are very active and in which a great many people are looking for minerals. Each man seeking minerals needs geological information. The department sent one small party into the Cariboo district last year. I assume their work has been valuable and will be available for miners next summer. I should like to be assured that there will be no suspension of that particular work in the current year.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask if there is any possibility of proceeding with a resurvey of the Nicola coal mines area. I have been asked by the Merritt board of trade to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, and should like to have some assurance from him that the work will be continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Answering the question and observations of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser), it is quite true that under the statutes the Dominion government has certain obligations with respect to carrying on geological work in British Columbia. I am not entirely unacquainted with the mineral industry of this country, and it would not need the impulse of statutory enactment to move me towards doing everything possible to supply what money is necessary in order to advance the interests of that great industry. I had in mind with respect to British Columbia, although it has not been definitely decided upon, as I pointed out a while ago, the placing of parties this summer at Bridge river, Cariboo, Kamloops, North Vancouver island and at Finlay river. That program may be subject to some change when the work of the coming summer is finally decided upon.
With respect to the questions put by the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) I would be the last one to disturb the very efficient staff that has been built up through the years in the geological survey. This reduction in the vote will not in any way interfere with that staff, but rather the parties in the field will be cut down and some of the staff who perhaps have not been engaged in actual field work will be used in that work this summer. That will have to be determined, but I can assure the hon. gentleman that the reduction will not affect the permanent staff here to which he has made reference. The reduction in the number of geological parties I trust will not continue during the years that follow, but confronted as this country is with very serious financial problems I have found a great willingness in the mineral industry, represented as it is by so many men active in carrying on that great work, to have economies made at this time, temporary-it is true, in order to relieve the taxpayer and the treasury to as large an extent as possible. I have had the matter up on a number of occasions with the representatives of the mineral industry, and they seemed to be quite
Supply-Mines

in accord with the efforts we are putting forward to exercise the greatest possible economy without injuring seriously the efficiency of the geological survey.
Mr. Chairman-
These are false economies, in my opinion-

With the consent of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), may I say, Mr. Chairman, that I regret in the discussion of these estimates that everybody gets up and asks a question out of tune and out of time so that it is impossible for an hon. member to get his questions and answers on the record in any intelligible way. I have sat here listening with interest to the discussion, and if my hon. friend from Macleod will allow me sufficient time to ask a question or two I shall be satisfied to sit down. I think it would help if hon. members would follow that practice for the sake of the record.
I wanted to ask the minister a question with regard to the next item, No. 162, for the publication of French and English editions of the reports, maps and illustrations. I notice that there is an increase of $15,000 in this item. Does that mean that there will be an increased publication in French? I gathered that the minister said a few moments ago that there was an increase in certain items because of certain publications. If the minister will increase items of this kind by fifty or sixty or seventy thousand dollars I shall have no objection to voting the money, provided that such publications as the one I hold in my hand, Les Oiseaux de Test du Canada-The Birds of Eastern Canada-by Doctor Taverner, be translated into French and distributed. I think that such reports and a report on the birds of western Canada should be translated into French, as well as various reports on the geological deposits in Canada, and if that were done I should have no objection to voting a larger amount than this, provided that the minister give us the assurance that the reports from the Mines branch will be put out to the public in French within a reasonable time. I know that the French calls for two operations and the English only one, but if the reports were published more nearly concurrently in French and English, I should be glad to vote any amount of money. It has been my privilege to see and to appreciate the work of the translation into French of some of the technical reports from the Mines branch, and I mention the Mines branch at this moment because only the estimates of that branch are under consideration at the moment. I have in mind some reports

of 250 and 350 pages, for instance, the report on the Rouyn district, which has been translated into French. It is astonishing to me that these reports are not more widely distributed amongst the colleges, universities and institutions of learning in Canada. I think the government, and I have said this on a number of other occasions, should take steps to see that these technical publications, on which such a tremendous amount of money is spent, and properly spent, are put into the hands of the proper educational institutions. I have in mind, if I am in order in mentioning it, a pamphlet published by the Department of Agriculture last year on beef and its uses, and the ways of cutting it. I distributed over six hundred copies of that pamphlet in the educational institutions of this city. We pay a tremendous amount of money for the compilation of these reports and a tremendous amount of money for their translation, and then unfortunately there is no activity shown in distributing them so that they may serve the purpose for which they are prepared. I have no hesitation in approving of this increase of $15,000 if the minister will say that it will mean an easier distribution of the publications in English and French of the editions of reports, maps, illustrations and so on, and that something will be done with a view to further distributing these educational reports among our institutions of learning.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not think that anyone will disagree with the observations that have been made by the senior member for Ottawa. This increase will take care of that work, covering the birds of both eastern and western Canada, and will also take care of an appropriate number of reports in the French language. In the department there has been built up, over a great number of years, a mailing list that covers universities, colleges and libraries of alii kinds, and reports that would seem to be suitable to these institutions are mailed to them. AVith respect to the publication of reports in the French language, that is now being done, not in its entirety it is true, because there are many reports in which, as I think the hon. member for Ottawa will agree on reflection, very few people in the province of Quebec would be interested; but those reports generally in which, in the opinion of the officers of the department and of myself, the people in that province, or in other French speaking parts of Canada, would be interested, are published in French. Take for instance the expansion in northeastern Quebec; the reports in that connection are printed in both English and French. I do not

Translations Bureau-Mr. Deslauriers
think however that the interest which would be taken in the province of Quebec in some other reports would really justify their publication in French. Certainly reports are now and have been for some time published in the French language, wherever, in the opinion of the department, they would usefully serve French speaking Canada. That practice, I think, is a proper one.

I understand the minister
to say, replying to the hon. member for Cariboo, that the first item here for geological explorations, surveys and investigations had been reduced by $44,000 because it was the desire of the government to effect economy. But the previous vote which the committee passed, for administration under national defence, was reduced by one per cent whereas, in this geological surveys vote, the reduction of $44,000 is equivalent to a 35 per cent cut, as compared with the amount voted last year.
I suggest that this is the wrong place to practice economy. It is false economy, at a time like this, to out down the amount spent on geological surveys. The object of these survey parties is to explore new areas particularly for the purpose of discovering any minerals that exist therein, and I believe that this offers at the present time some hope for employment in new industries. I think we should encourage the opening up of new mineral areas in Canada.
I would express my appreciation of the service I have received from the geological surveys branch on different occasions; but this year when I inquired for certain maps of districts in the northwest territories I was informed that no surveys had yet been made of some of those districts. I think the government might very well increase rather than decrease the vote for surveys, particularly in that territory. Some new gold fields might be found, and the production of gold in Canada would help us to discharge the foreign debt which worries us so much.
Will the minister tell me how this vote of $83,000 compares with the same vote for the last four or five years? Is not this a steady cutting-down of the amount spent on geological surveys, and after all is it not false economy? In what better way could the government spend money now than in opening up new mineral areas in Canada? Are there not districts in the Northwest Territories, where metals are now being discovered, in which the department has not yet made regular surveys and issued maps of the districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order
to carry out the arrangement made on Friday night, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

The house resumed from Friday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cahan for the second reading of Bill No. 4, respecting the bureau for translations and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Chevrier.

Mr. Speaker, this measure
known as the "Bureau for Translations Act" is submitted for our consideration, under the plea of economy and efficiency. The speeches, however, to which we have listened, proved that economy and efficiency were not at stake in this bill. Experience has shown that this system had been tried in other countries and found wanting.
I shall not, this evening, attempt to repeat the arguments presented to the house against this bill. I shall discuss another aspect of the question. Relying on my experience as a parliamentarian of long standing, may I state that it is an easy matter for me to observe, at present, that all conservative regimes when they apprehend that their end is near, always resort, before going out of office, to a reorganization scheme of this nature. Is it, this year as in the past, a sign of approaching elections? We expect so. Once, in the past, it was the civil service reorganization. As ever, with economy and efficiency of the service as their aim, the Civil Service Commission sprung up. This institution, as all know, is a great drag on the country and its mechanism has had an entire different result from the one expected. I had often the occasion of expressing my views on this institution and its effects. I shall, this evening, summarize my thoughts in this respect by stating again that it is an institution in which political influence, by indirect means, has its elbow-room and, in which the staff is recruited mostly on the grounds of friendship, relationship and sometimes loveship. Owing to this institution, the representatives of the people have seen their prerogatives decrease and have been so checked that they can hardly be of service to those that have given them a mandate.
I am aware, and I have heard it stated, recently, in the house, that the question of patronage is held in horror by certain members. They prefer not to be pestered by

Translations Bureau-Mr. Deslauriers
people who seek privileges, positions or a service. However, after all, I think it is incumbent on a member, owing to his mandate, to look after legitimate requests and claims of those who have entrusted him with this mandate. And the fact of replying that what they request is entirely out of his hands, that it is within the purview of an independent institution, which has the authority over their request or desire, cannot possibly satisfy those interested. The representative who wishes to fulfil his duty, in my opinion, can not be satisfied with the part he plays.
Later on, always on the eve of an election, we had the Young classification, which had very little results; then came the Griffenhagen reorganization. If we question, always from an efficient and economic viewpoint, the people, especially the French Canadians of Ottawa, we find that the latter always lost many of their rights.
Now, so far as efficiency, after these thorough reorganizations, it certainly has not improved since the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), discovered in the course of his numerous travels, stacks of French publications valued at hundreds of thousands of dollars which were not distributed. It is admitted that the only and unique reason was that these bundles of publications were out of date, issued at a time when no one required them, because the English version had been issued long before, and, therefore, the French version had become useless. Consequently, no efficiency resulted from such an organization, and we have every reason to believe that such a departure, this year, will have the same result.
Are you censuring the hon. member for Labelle?

If the hon. member will kindly let me proceed, he will be in a position to know whether I am censuring him or not.
The hon. member for Labelle is supporting the measure. He quotes figures which are not official but confidential, and he endeavours to prove that the translators do not earn their salaries, besides being the cause of all the evil inherent to the questions relating to French in our parliament.
May I, sir, express a totally opposite view. First, the figures he quoted are not official, therefore they are difficult to contradict since they are confidential. On the other hand, we are obliged to take them for what they are worth. They are not official, since the hon. Secretary of State stated, replying to a question put by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. St. Pere) that these figures were not
lMr. Deslauriers.]
issued by his department or by himself, directly or indirectly. The following are the figures quoted by the hon. member for Labelle. I think we must take the word of the hon. Secretary of State in his reply to the hon. member for Hochelaga. First, if he had in his department translators unemployed, he would certainly be aware of it. If there were work to be done in his department, as one who attends to his duties, as we all know, he would certainly have given out the work to these unemployed officials. We are aware, on both sides of the house, that the hon. Secretary of State has certain work of his department done by outsiders. If there were translators unemployed in his department he would, first, utilize them instead of giving out the work.
In quoting these confidential figures, the hon. member for Labelle stated that in the Department of Agriculture seven translators, in the course of a year, had translated but 568 pages each; in the Immigration department, two translators had only translated, in the same period, 46 pages each; in the Public Works department, three translators had only translated 108 pages; in the Mines department, three other translators 148, and in the Trade and Commerce, four translators 1,719. Dealing with the unreliability-may I say-of the figures quoted by the hon. member for Labelle-because it is inconceivable that a man, in the course of a year's work, succeeded, without dying of languor, in translating only 46 pages -dealing with the unlikelihood of such figures, I took the pains to obtain a confidential, not official list, of the departments of Agriculture, Immigration, Public Works, Mines and Trade and Commerce, and what is very strange, the information obtained greatly differs from that of the hon. member for Labelle. For instance, in the Agriculture department, seven translators translated 742 pages, each; in the Immigration, instead of 46 pages, the two translators had to their credit 568 pages and, in the Public Works department, three translators, 715 pages. In the Mines department, where the work is exceedingly difficult owing to the technical subjects, the three translators translated 572 pages. In the Trade and Commerce department, instead of 1,700 and a few pages, there were 1,425 pages of similar schedule work.
Seeing that our figures differ entirely, it would be interesting to have the hon. Secretary of State appoint a committee of members, so that those interested could give evidence as to the amount of work they have accomplished during the period mentioned, and, thereby discover whether in the figures they quote the hon. member for Labelle is

Translations Bureau-Mr. Deslauriers
nearer to the truth than the hon. member for St. Mary's. This procedure would entail no delay and permit the house to give, perhaps, a more intelligent vote on this bill. Another important point, as the interested parties have not been heard, this committee would afford them an opportunity-which would be highly appreciated-of defending themselves against those who insult them and proving their gratitude to those who wish to do them justice.
According to the statement of the hon. member for Labelle, the stenographers of the House of Commons should be placed in the same class.
One must have very little knowledge of what takes place in the house to make such a statement. Both sides of the house are aware that to find a qualified French stenographer, the Civil Service Commission held a number of tests and that all of them, without exception proved a failure, owing to the difficulty of obtaining qualified men. I may even state that a number of official court stenographers, those who take down court evidence, have failed when put to the test, here. Disheartened, after a few days of trial, they were forced to return home and take up their work in the courts, where their remuneration is higher than that received at present, by the Hansard stenographers of the house. Yet, we heard an hon. member state in the house that the government is at liberty to dictate whatever terms they please to stenographers of the house. I state that if the Civil Service Commission, after a number of tests, were unable to find one qualified person, the government is not at liberty to dictate whatever terms they please to these officials.

Hear,
hear!

Now, sir, may I somewhat discuss the question of the translators of the House of Commons, with whom I have the pleasure of being better acquainted than with the others. I had, personally, the opportunity on numerous occasions, since I am in parliament, to see them at their work, translating technical subjects which I had brought up in the house, such, for instances, electrifying our railways, occupational or trade disability, tuberculous cattle, the question of fruit and vegetable sprinkling, and the regulations which govern this trade abroad. All these subjects embody numerous formulas of industrial, organic and inorganic chemistry, etc., and I am able to state to the house that their work, in so difficult a field, which obliged them at times not only to show much patience, but also to
make researches devoid of any interest, was perfect, and I wish to bear witness of my appreciation.

Hear,
hear!

May I, sir, in support of my contention, borrow one of the arguments of the hon. member for Labelle. This may seem somewhat paradoxical since he made use of it to prove quite the opposite. The argument of the hon. member for Labelle is as follows: He was obliged, at times, to pause two hours in searching for the-exact term which would express his thought. I am willing to believe him, although I confess that it must have been an extraordinary thought, for, in the natural course of events,

At all events, if it took him two hours to translate his thought, what merit must the translators of the house have when they must translate the thoughts of others, which is much more difficult! What merit must these men have? That is why I think that his argument may be retorted. If it be so deserving of praise to be a translator, why then criticize the translators, especially those of the House of Commons.
When the thought is not there, it cannot be translated!

Perhaps, I admit.
I have been, sir, a general practitioner for thirty years-and when called upon between sessions, I still oarry on-and I have had the opportunity of treating, among my clients, workers in various occupations; industrial workers, printers and hand labourers. In my career as a medical man, I observed that although they are all workers, there are, among them, people who are entitled, in all fairness, to higher salaries than those of their neighbour. To illustrate somewhat my argument, may I take, for instance, the printer who constantly comes in contact with anti-monj' salts and who is compelled to retire at 45 years old; because his sight is defective. This man whose eyesight is affected at such an early age is entitled to a higher salary than the one who can earn a livelihood up to 60 or 70 years old. The same applies to polishers of copper and various metals. I now come, sir, to the brain worker who is obliged to accomplish ihis work at continuous high tension. It is unfair to wish to relegate him with his colleagues in offices so as to exact from him, during 12 months, mercenary work,

with a decreased salary. I entirely disagree with such views. We have witnessed in our educational institutions, in our colleges and universities, students whose health has been ruined by over work, men hardly having reached ripe age, become sometimes the victims of this brain overwork. I think there is, at present, legislation being enacted which will force a class of workers, who are worthy of all our sympathy and who certainly earn their salaries to adopt this manner of living. I intend to vote against this measure, because, in my opinion, economy no more than efficiency are at stake. I am rather inclined to think that it is a sign of an approaching election, that the present administration, already on its last leg, wish to erect themselves a small monument to remind us of its regime, in case they were refused a return ticket at the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with much interest the speeches delivered, on both sides of the house, on the second reading of bill No. 4, introduced by the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). From the viewpoint of the French language, numerous arguments have been set forth, and I think we all agree on the subject. The hon. Solicitor general (Mr. Dupre), if I am not mistaken, endeavoured to prove, just now, that bill No. 4 constituted a complement to section 133 of the British North America Act. Although the letter of the law is not very precise as to the use of the French language and the publication in French of the various official documents of Canada, we have always been under the impression since confederation, and especially within the last twenty years, that the French language was to occupy a place of honour in this country. Translators were appointed in all departments. That was an official recognition of the French language. These translators, scattered here and there, over the government departments, occupy, each of them, a place of honour and translate not only the documents of their departments but often those of other departments when their special qualifications are required. They were, so to speak, the French ornament of each department, and they are still. They accomplished their task scrupulously. Perhaps, defects appeared, at times, but this is not a reason to blame the system. There are no rules without exception, if in such and such a department unqualified translators are met with, let them be replaced. However, one must not, for such a reason, upset the entire system of translation and concentrate them in a large study hall.
It is stated that one of the advantages of the act will be to ensure the simultaneous publication of English and French documents. I respectfully submit that this is a myth. They must first be printed in English before the translators begin their work. Complaints come from the government side that docu-
ments, proceedings and departmental reports were not translated in sufficient numbers or when required. It must be that the departments were short of men or of qualified persons. Yet, we find in the explanatory notes that this bill is introduced to obtain more efficiency and to economize the public moneys.

Then if you wish to have a larger output of translated reports and obtain the object which the Solicitor General mentioned, more translators will be required and, therefore, it will be at a greater cost to the country. AH have complained, for twenty years, under all administrations, of the small number of translated publications. If you wish to have a larger number of these, additional translators will be required, the cost will increase, as a greater efficiency can not be obtained at a lower cost; the two clash.
